blurb: The engine under every AI model, from scratch: what a neuron does, how a network measures its mistakes, and how it fixes them.

lessons.title: A neuron is a weighted vote

cards.title: From one neuron to a network

steps.p: An artificial neuron takes some numbers in, multiplies each by a weight (how much it matters), adds them up, and outputs one number.
Learning means adjusting the weights. A big positive weight says "this input pushes yes"; a negative one says "this pushes no".
steps.analogy: Deciding whether to go out: the weather, your mood and your wallet each get a say, some louder than others.

steps.p: Each neuron's output then goes through a simple bend, like ReLU: keep positives, turn negatives into zero. This is the activation function.
Without it, stacking any number of layers collapses into one simple straight-line rule. The bends let networks learn curved, complex patterns.
Many neurons form a layer; layers feed into layers. Early layers find simple patterns, later ones combine them into complex ideas.

cards.q: What does a single artificial neuron do?
options: Multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up and outputs one number
cards.hint: Look at the flow in step 1.
cards.why: Weigh, add, output. That's all one neuron does. Intelligence comes from billions of them with well-tuned weights.

cards.statement: Stacking ten layers with no activation functions gives a more powerful model than one layer.
cards.why: False. Without bends, ten straight-line layers combine into one straight-line rule. The activation functions are what add power.

cards.q: ReLU largely replaced the S-shaped sigmoid in deep networks mainly because…
options: It keeps learning signals strong instead of shrinking them toward zero
cards.why: Signals don't fade. The sigmoid flattens out at both ends, so training signals shrink through many layers. ReLU's slope stays at 1 for positive inputs.

cards.title: A 1969 book proving simple one-layer networks couldn't learn XOR helped trigger the first AI winter.
cards.detail: Minsky and Papert's "Perceptrons" showed single-layer networks can't solve problems like "one or the other but not both". Multi-layer networks can, but nobody knew how to train them yet.

cards.statement: A single-layer network can learn "one or the other, but not both" (XOR).
cards.why: False. No single straight line can separate those cases. You need at least one hidden layer with a bend.

steps.p: After each prediction, the loss scores how wrong the network was. Training's whole aim is to make that score smaller.
steps.analogy: Like a golf score: lower is better.

steps.p: For each weight, work out whether nudging it up or down would lower the loss, and how much. Together these are the gradient.
steps.analogy: Standing on a foggy hillside: you can't see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet.

steps.p: Nudge every weight a little in its downhill direction. The step size is the learning rate.

visual.caption: Loss falls fast at first, then levels off.

steps.h: Not too big, not too small
steps.p: Too big a step overshoots the valley and the loss bounces or explodes. Too small and training crawls.
Instead of checking the whole dataset before each step, use a small random batch. It's noisier but vastly faster. That's stochastic gradient descent.

cards.q: What usually happens if the learning rate is far too high?
options: The loss bounces around or explodes instead of falling
cards.hint: Giant leaps on a foggy hillside.
cards.why: Overshooting. Each step jumps past the low point, often landing higher than before.

options: For each weight, which way and how much to nudge it to reduce the loss
cards.why: The downhill direction. One number per weight, telling training how to adjust it.

cards.statement: Stochastic gradient descent checks the entire dataset before each update.
cards.why: False. It uses a small random batch each step — "stochastic" means random. Many quick, rough steps beat a few slow perfect ones.

cards.title: The popular Adam optimizer stores two extra numbers for every parameter.
cards.detail: It tracks a running average of each weight's recent gradients and of their size. For a model with billions of parameters, that's many extra gigabytes.

cards.q: Perplexity 10 means a model is roughly as unsure as…
options: Choosing evenly among 10 equally likely next words
cards.why: A 10-way coin toss. Perplexity turns loss into an intuitive "how many options is it torn between". Lower is better.

steps.p: Data flows forward through the layers to produce a prediction, and the loss is calculated.
Starting from the loss, the error is passed backwards layer by layer, working out how much each weight contributed to the mistake.

items: Backward: share out the blame layer by layer

steps.p: Each layer passes blame to the layer before, in proportion to how much it relied on it.
steps.analogy: A team project goes wrong: the manager traces back who contributed what, passing responsibility down the chain.

steps.p: One backward pass gives the gradient for every weight at once — about twice the work of the forward pass. So training costs about 3× a forward pass.
Libraries like PyTorch work out the backward pass automatically. You only write the forward calculation.

cards.statement: Backpropagation needs the results from the forward pass kept in memory.
cards.why: True. To share out blame, it needs each layer's results from the forward pass. That's a big part of training's memory use.

cards.q: Training compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens. About how much for a 7-billion-parameter model on 1 trillion tokens?
cards.why: About 4.2 × 10²². 6 × 7 = 42, and 10⁹ × 10¹² = 10²¹. The 6 is 2 for the forward pass plus 4 for the backward pass.

cards.q: In backpropagation, which direction does the error travel?
options: Backwards, from the output toward the input
cards.why: Backwards. The loss is known at the output, so blame is passed back through the layers from there.

cards.title: Backpropagation was made famous by a 1986 paper — but invented earlier, more than once.
cards.detail: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularised it. Seppo Linnainmaa described the core maths in 1970, and Paul Werbos proposed using it for neural networks in the 1970s.

cards.statement: In PyTorch, you must write the gradient formula for every layer you create.
cards.why: False. It records the forward calculation and works out gradients automatically. That convenience helped deep learning spread.

cards.title: Did it learn, or just memorise?

steps.p: Split the data: train on most, keep some aside the model never trains on. Score on that held-back set to see how it does on new examples.
A model can memorise its training examples perfectly yet do badly on new ones.
steps.analogy: A student who memorised last year's exam answers but can't handle a new question.

steps.p: If training loss keeps falling while held-back loss starts rising, the model has started memorising.
Tricks like dropout — randomly switching off some neurons during training — stop the network relying on any single path.
The test set is used once, at the end. Tuning settings by peeking at it quietly turns it into training data.

options: Randomly switching off some neurons during training
cards.why: Random switch-offs. The network can't rely on any one neuron, so it learns sturdier, more general patterns.

cards.statement: It's fine to tune your model's settings by checking results on the test set.
cards.hint: The test set is a final exam.
cards.why: False. Then the test score is no longer a fair measure of new data. Use the validation set for tuning.

cards.q: Training loss keeps falling but held-back loss starts rising. What's happening?
options: The model is memorising instead of learning general patterns
The data is too small to measure
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 3.
cards.why: Overfitting. It's getting better at its practice questions and worse at new ones. Time to stop, or add regularisation.

cards.title: Some networks suddenly generalise long after they've perfectly memorised their training data — "grokking".
cards.detail: Power et al. (2022) trained small transformers on clock arithmetic. Scores on new data stayed near chance for thousands of steps after training was perfect, then suddenly jumped to near 100%.

cards.q: Why use a separate validation set as well as a test set?
options: Tune settings on validation, so the test set stays a fair final check
Because more sets are always better
cards.why: Keep the final exam unseen. Validation is for practice and adjusting; test is the one honest score at the end.
